note: Plain-English explanations in three levels: 'simple' (the concept, using normal super terms such as pre-tax and after-tax), 'standard' (the rule and key numbers, in the order a member needs them) and 'detailed' (the full rule, worked examples and edge cases). A level is a list of blocks. A plain string is a numbered step: a logic chain where each step follows from the one before, or instructions in order. Where a numbered list would blur together, use {lead} (an unnumbered lead-in), {options:[{name,text}], label?} (side-by-side choices), {table:{head,rows}}, {example} or {note}. 'links' go to the calculator, checklists, rules, forms, timeframes and other explainers. 'source' is the PDS (one quote or a list); 'also' holds supplementary ATO or UniSuper website quotes. 'general' marks where general information stops and advice would start. Every dollar figure must exist in rates.json, the source or 'also' quotes, or allow_numbers (check-data.mjs enforces this). 'terms' get a hover-over wherever they appear in a card.

items.title: Minimum annual payment
simple: A pension must pay you at least a minimum amount each financial year. It's a government rule.
The minimum is a percentage of your balance on 1 July, and the percentage rises with age.
You can take more than the minimum, but never less.
standard: On 1 July each year we take your balance and multiply it by the factor for your age.
That's the least you must be paid that financial year. You can choose more (up to 10% if it's a TTR pension).
Extra withdrawals during the year don't lower that year's minimum. It's worked out again next 1 July.

standard.note: In the year a pension starts, the minimum is pro-rated to the days left (see First-year pro-rata minimum).

detailed: The minimum is set once, at the start of each financial year: balance on 1 July × the age-based factor.

detailed.example: At 70 with $400,000 on 1 July the factor is 5%, so the minimum is $20,000 for the year, about $1,670 a month.

detailed: Extra withdrawals during the year don't reduce that year's minimum.
In the year a pension starts, the minimum is pro-rated to the days left. From the next 1 July the full-year rule applies.

detailed.note: Closing a pension, or moving it back to super, part-way through a year: the pro-rata minimum up to that date has to be paid first.

items.general: Explain how the minimum is worked out. Don't suggest how much above the minimum to take.

source.quote: Your minimum income amount is calculated by multiplying your opening account balance by your age-based percentage factor at the start of each financial year

items.title: First-year pro-rata minimum
simple: The minimum is a yearly amount that assumes the pension runs from 1 July to 30 June.
A pension that starts part-way through the year only runs for part of it.
So in the first year, the minimum is reduced in proportion to the days left until 30 June.
standard: Start with the full-year minimum: starting balance × the factor for your age.
Count the days from your start date to 30 June, including the start date.
Multiply the full-year minimum by the days left, divide by the days in the year, and round to the nearest ten dollars.
That's your minimum for this first year. From the next 1 July it's a full-year amount on that day's balance.

standard.note: If you start between 1 June and 30 June, you can choose not to be paid until the next financial year.

detailed: Full-year minimum = starting balance × age factor.
Pro-rate it by the days left in the financial year, counting the start date.

detailed.example: Aged 67, $500,000, starting 1 October: 5% gives $25,000 for a full year. 273 of 365 days are left, so $25,000 × 273 ÷ 365 = $18,698.63, rounded to $18,700.

detailed: The TTR maximum isn't pro-rated, so in a TTR pension's first year the range runs from the pro-rated minimum to the full 10%.

detailed.note: Starting between 1 June and 30 June: the member can choose no payment until the next financial year.

detailed: From 1 July the full-year rule applies, using the balance on that day.
items.general: Explain the calculation. Don't advise on the start date or amount.

source.quote: $25,000 (minimum amount) × 273 (days remaining in the financial year) ÷ 365 = $18,698.63

items.title: TTR compared with Retirement Phase
simple: Super is normally preserved until you retire. A TTR pension lets you draw some of it from preservation age (60) while you keep working.
Because you're still working, it has limits: at most 10% a year, generally no lump sums, and earnings are still taxed.
Once you retire or turn 65, it becomes a Retirement Phase pension and those limits fall away.
standard: At 65 a TTR pension becomes a Retirement Phase pension automatically.
Before 65, it converts once you tell us you've retired or met another condition of release, such as leaving a job from 60.

head: TTR pension
Retirement Phase pension
rows: Minimum to 10% of the 1 July (or opening) balance
Not when a TTR pension starts
May apply when money moves in

detailed: Conversion happens at 65, or once the member tells us they've met a condition of release, such as retiring or ending a job from 60.
On conversion the balance counts towards the transfer balance cap, the 10% maximum falls away, and earnings become tax-free.
items.general: Explain the differences. Whether TTR suits someone's tax or work situation is advice: refer to UniSuper Advice.

source.quote: Once you reach age 65 or let us know you've met a condition of release allowing unrestricted access to your super (e.g. retired from the workforce or terminate employment from age 60), your TTR Flexi Pension will be converted into a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension

items.title: The TTR 10% maximum
simple: A TTR pension can pay at most 10% of its balance each financial year.
Unlike the minimum, that 10% isn't reduced when the pension starts part-way through the year.
So a late start means the full 10% is available over fewer months.
standard: The maximum is 10% of your balance on 1 July, or of your starting balance in the first year.
The minimum is pro-rated in the first year, but the maximum isn't.
So if you start late in the year, you can still take the full 10% before 30 June.
Unless you choose otherwise, it's spread evenly over the months that are left.
The maximum only applies while it's TTR. It falls away when the pension converts to Retirement Phase.
detailed: The maximum is 10% of the 1 July balance, or of the opening balance in the first year.
It isn't pro-rated, so a late start keeps the full 10%.

detailed.example: A $400,000 TTR pension started in April can pay up to $40,000 before 30 June: $13,330 a month for April, May and June.

detailed: Once the pension converts to Retirement Phase, there's no maximum at all.
items.general: Explain the limit. Don't suggest an amount.

source.quote: The maximum amount for TTR Flexi Pension isn't subject to the pro-rata rules.

items.title: Why money can't be added to a pension
simple: A pension starts with a single amount, and the law doesn't allow anything to be added to it afterwards.
New money, whether contributions or rollovers, goes into a super (accumulation) account instead.
From there it can start a second pension, or be combined with the first by restarting it.
standard: Once a pension starts, nothing more can be added. It's a legal requirement.
So any new contribution or rollover goes into a super account first. From there you have two choices:

options.name: Start a second pension
options.text: Keep the existing pension and start a new one with the new money. Each has its own minimum and its own tax components.

options.name: Restart as one pension
options.text: Move the existing pension back to super, combine it with the new money and start one new pension. The pro-rata minimum on the old pension has to be paid first.

standard.note: That's why we suggest bringing all your super together before starting, after checking you won't lose insurance in another fund.

detailed: Once a Flexi Pension starts, no further amounts can be added: a legal requirement.
New money has to go into an accumulation account first.

options.name: Second pension
options.text: Start a new Flexi Pension with the new money. Separate minimum, separate tax components, and both count towards the transfer balance cap if they're Retirement Phase pensions (a TTR pension doesn't count).

options.name: Restart
options.text: Commute the existing pension back to super, combine, and start one new pension. The pro-rata minimum to the closure date is paid first, and the new pension gets a new start date and a new first-year minimum.

detailed.note: Before consolidating, check insurance in any fund the money is coming from.

items.general: Explain the rule. Whether to consolidate first, or open a second pension, can be a personal decision.

source.quote: Once you start a Flexi Pension, you can't add further amounts to it. If you want to add money to an existing Flexi Pension account, you'll have to start a new account. This is a legal requirement.

items.title: Transfer balance cap
simple: Investment earnings in a retirement pension are tax-free, so there's a lifetime limit on how much you can move into retirement pensions.
That limit is the transfer balance cap: $2.1 million for someone starting their first retirement pension now.
It counts what you move in, not later investment growth, and the ATO keeps track of it.
standard: The transfer balance cap is a lifetime limit on how much you can move into retirement-phase pensions, across all your funds.
For a first retirement pension now it's $2.1 million. If you started one earlier, your personal cap may be between $1.6 and $2.1 million.

head: Counts against the cap
Frees up cap
No effect

Lump sum withdrawals from a retirement pension
Investment growth or losses, and regular pension payments

standard: The ATO tracks it, so your exact cap and balance are in ATO online services.
detailed: The transfer balance cap limits the total moved into retirement-phase pensions over a lifetime. The ATO tracks it in the member's transfer balance account.
The general cap is $2.1 million. Members who started a retirement pension earlier have a personal cap between $1.6 and $2.1 million.

head: Counts against the cap
Frees up cap
No effect
rows: Money moved into a Retirement Phase pension, a TTR pension when it converts, and the Retirement Bonus
Lump sum withdrawals from a retirement pension
Investment growth or losses, and regular pension payments

detailed.example: Moving $1.5 million in leaves about $600,000 of cap for future pensions, even if the pension grows.

detailed.note: Over the cap, the ATO can require the excess to be removed, with tax on it. The member's cap and balance are in ATO online services.

items.general: Explain the cap. A member's own cap and options if they're near it: ATO, and advice.

source.quote: To view your transfer balance cap and your transfer balance account, please contact the ATO or log in to the ATO's online services via ato.gov.au.

items.title: Retirement Bonus
simple: In super and TTR pensions, we set aside part of your investment earnings for capital gains tax we may have to pay later.
In a Retirement Phase pension earnings are tax-free, so some of that money isn't needed.
Eligible members get it as a Retirement Bonus, added automatically when their Retirement Phase pension starts.

simple.note: If you take out 50% or more of the pension's starting balance within 12 months, the bonus can be taken back.

standard: The Retirement Bonus passes on capital gains tax set aside in super that isn't needed once money moves into a tax-free Retirement Phase pension. It's added automatically when the pension starts.

head: How it works
rows: Anyone moving money into a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension from 1 October 2026, after 12 continuous months with money in a UniSuper super account (DBD included) or TTR pension.
Money from eligible investment options. Cash, Australian Bond and Australian Income are excluded; pre-mixed options count in full.
The amount moved from eligible options × the bonus rate (0.7% on the website, 13 Nov 2026).
Yes: a bonus each time a new Retirement Phase pension starts, up to $14,700 in total across all accounts.
Withdraw 50% or more of the pension's starting balance within 12 months of it starting, and the bonus can be deducted from the pension.

standard.example: Moving $500,000 from eligible options gives a $3,500 bonus.

detailed: In super and TTR, UniSuper provides for future capital gains tax. Retirement Phase earnings are tax-free, so part of that provision isn't needed and may be passed on.
Money moves from super, TTR or DBD into a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension, from 1 October 2026.

Money has been in a UniSuper super account or TTR pension for a continuous 12 months before the transfer. The 12 months starts when money first reaches the account (not when it's opened), can be counted across several accounts, and excludes time in a Retirement Phase account.
The money is in eligible investment options. Cash, Australian Bond and Australian Income are excluded; a pre-mixed option counts in full, even though it holds some of those assets.

detailed.lead: Amount: the amount moved from eligible options × the bonus rate on the start date (0.7% on the website, 13 Nov 2026).

detailed.example: $750,000 moved, of which $150,000 is in Cash: only $600,000 counts, so the bonus is $4,200.

options.name: More than one bonus
options.text: One for each new Retirement Phase pension, up to a lifetime total of $14,700 per member across all accounts.

options.name: Clawback
options.text: If 50% or more of the pension's starting balance is withdrawn within 12 months of it starting, the Trustee can deduct the bonus. Mention this when a member asks for a large lump sum in the first year.

options.name: Caps
options.text: It isn't a contribution, so contribution caps don't apply. It does count towards the transfer balance cap.

detailed.note: The bonus is at the Trustee's discretion and can change or stop without notice. Don't promise an amount: refer to unisuper.com.au/retirement-bonus.

items.general: Explain eligibility. Don't estimate a specific bonus amount: refer to unisuper.com.au/retirement-bonus.

source.quote: The Retirement Bonus represents tax savings that may be passed on to eligible members when they start a Retirement Phase Flexi Pension.
If you withdraw 50% or more of your opening balance within 12 months of starting your Retirement Phase Flexi Pension, the Trustee may claw back the Retirement Bonus.

also.quote: There's no limit to how many times you can receive a Retirement Bonus. For example, you could receive another if you open a new Flexi Pension later. However, the total you can receive across all your accounts is capped at $14,700.
If you withdraw 50% or more of your Flexi Pension starting balance within 12 months of opening the account, we reserve the right to deduct the Retirement Bonus from your Flexi Pension.
Your Retirement Bonus is calculated as: the amount you transfer from eligible investment options × 0.7% bonus rate.

items.title: Drawdown order

simple.lead: If your pension is spread across investment options, you choose which options your payments come from. There are three ways:

options.name: Default
options.text: Cash first, then the more conservative options, then growth.

options.name: Your choice
options.text: You set the order.

options.name: Pro-rata
options.text: A share from every option, in proportion to its balance.

standard.lead: Each pension payment has to come out of your investment options. You choose one of three drawdown methods:

options.name: Default order
options.text: Cash first, then the more conservative options, then the growth options.

options.name: Your choice
options.text: You set the order the options are used in.

options.name: Pro-rata
options.text: Every payment comes from every option, in proportion to how much is in each.

standard: With the default order or your choice, the options used first run down, so your mix shifts over time. Pro-rata keeps the mix the same.

standard.example: With 20% in Cash and 80% in Balanced, pro-rata takes each payment 20% from Cash and 80% from Balanced. The default uses up the Cash first.

standard.note: Which method suits you is an investment decision.

options.name: Default order
options.text: Cash, then the remaining options from most to least conservative. Defensive assets are used first, so the mix drifts towards growth.

options.name: Your choice
options.text: The member sets the sequence. The mix drifts towards whichever options are last.

options.name: Pro-rata
options.text: In proportion to the amount in each option at the time of payment, so the asset mix stays as it is.

detailed.example: With 20% in Cash and 80% in Balanced, pro-rata takes each payment 20/80; the default uses up the Cash first.

detailed: Members can change the method online or with the Manage your investment choices form.

detailed.note: Recommending a method is investment advice: refer to UniSuper Advice.

items.general: Explain the methods. Which suits the member is an investment decision.

source.quote: Pro-rata – payments are drawn in proportion to the amount held in each investment option at the time of payment.

items.title: Temporary account before a pension starts
simple: When a pension application is waiting for super from other funds, the money is held in a temporary Accumulation 1 account.
It stays there, invested in Cash, until everything arrives or 90 days pass.
Then the account closes and the pension starts with the full amount.
standard: When you're rolling in super from other funds, we hold it in a temporary Accumulation 1 account.
It has no admin fees and no insurance, and it's invested in Cash so the amount stays steady.
It closes, and your pension starts, once all transfers have arrived, or 90 days after the first one, whichever comes first.
Anything arriving after that stays in super, because a pension can't be added to once it starts.
detailed: A temporary Accumulation 1 account holds rollovers and contributions while a Flexi Pension application waits for them.
It has no administration fees and no insurance, and it's invested in Cash.
It closes, and the pension begins, once all transfers are received and processed, or 90 days after the first one arrives, whichever happens first.
Amounts that arrive later stay in super, because nothing can be added to a pension once it starts.

detailed.note: If the pension isn't set up within 90 days, or part of the balance is left behind, it becomes a standard Accumulation 1 account and admin fees apply.

items.general: Factual.

source.quote: The temporary Accumulation 1 account will automatically close and your Flexi Pension will begin once we've received and processed all transfers and/or contributions, or 90 days after we receive the first transfer or contribution, whichever happens first.

items.title: The $10,000 close-out
simple: A pension keeps paying until its balance falls to $10,000.
At that point the rest is paid out and the pension closes.
Where it goes depends on the type: to your bank account for Retirement Phase, back to super for TTR.
standard: Your pension keeps paying until the balance falls to $10,000. Then we pay out the rest and close it. Where it goes depends on the type:

options.name: Retirement Phase or beneficiary pension
options.text: The rest is paid to your bank account.

options.name: TTR pension
options.text: The rest goes back into a super account, because TTR money is still preserved.

standard: How long it takes to reach $10,000 depends on your balance, payments, withdrawals, returns and fees.
detailed: The pension continues until the balance reduces to $10,000, then it's closed.

options.name: Retirement Phase and BIS
options.text: The remainder is paid as a lump sum to the nominated bank account.

options.name: TTR
options.text: The remainder is rolled back to an accumulation account, because the money is still preserved.

detailed.note: When that happens can't be worked out here: it depends on balance, payments, withdrawals, returns and fees. Refer to the Retirement income calculator or advice.

items.general: Factual. How long a pension will last is a projection: refer to the Retirement income calculator or advice.

source.quote: Your Flexi Pension will continue until the balance reduces to $10,000

items.title: Concessional and non-concessional contributions
simple: Concessional contributions are pre-tax: employer contributions, salary sacrifice, and personal contributions you claim a tax deduction for. The fund taxes them at 15%.
Non-concessional contributions are after-tax: money you add from your take-home pay or savings without claiming a deduction. No tax going in.
Each type has its own yearly cap, and going over can mean extra tax.
standard: The difference is whether the money has already been taxed.

head: Concessional (pre-tax)
Non-concessional (after-tax)
rows: Employer contributions, salary sacrifice, and personal contributions you claim as a deduction
Personal contributions you don't claim, and spouse contributions

standard: A personal contribution starts out after-tax. A notice of intent, acknowledged by us, turns it into a pre-tax contribution.

standard.note: Going over either cap can mean extra tax.

head: Concessional (pre-tax)
Non-concessional (after-tax)

Personal contributions you don't claim, and spouse contributions

detailed.example: $5,000 from savings, not claimed: non-concessional. Notice of intent lodged and acknowledged: concessional.

detailed.note: Excess concessional contributions that aren't released count towards the non-concessional cap.

items.title: Notice of intent to claim a deduction
simple: Personal after-tax contributions can be claimed as a tax deduction, which turns them into concessional (pre-tax) contributions.
To claim, you lodge a notice of intent with us and get our acknowledgement before claiming in your tax return.
It has to happen before the money is moved, withdrawn, split or used to start a pension.
standard: Make the personal contribution.
Lodge a notice of intent online, under Manage account.
Wait for our written acknowledgement.
Claim the deduction in your tax return. We deduct 15% contributions tax, and the amount counts towards your concessional cap.

standard.note: Lodge the notice before your tax return and by the end of the next financial year, and before any of that money is rolled over, withdrawn, split or used to start a pension. Otherwise the deduction can't be claimed in full.

detailed: A personal contribution stays non-concessional until a valid notice of intent is lodged and acknowledged in writing.
Once acknowledged, it's treated as a concessional contribution: 15% contributions tax, and it counts towards the concessional cap.

The notice must come before

Any of the contribution being rolled over, withdrawn, split to a spouse or used to start a pension

items.title: Contribution splitting
simple: Contribution splitting moves some of your pre-tax (concessional) contributions from last financial year into your spouse's super.
Once it's transferred, the money belongs to your spouse. It's part of their balance, and they can only access it when they meet a condition of release.
It still counts towards your concessional cap, not theirs.
standard: Wait for the financial year to end: you split last year's concessional contributions, once a year.
Check your spouse can receive it: under 60, or 60 to 64 and not retired. Not at 65 or over.
Work out the amount: up to 85% of last year's concessional contributions (and no more than your cap).
If you're claiming a deduction on any of it, lodge the notice of intent first.
Send the request so it reaches us by 30 June.

head: After the split
You
Your spouse
rows: Your spouse: it's in their account
When they meet a condition of release

detailed: Splittable: the previous financial year's concessional contributions (employer, salary sacrifice, deducted personal). Not non-concessional contributions, rollovers or co-contributions.
Maximum: the lesser of 85% of those contributions and the concessional cap.
Spouse: under 60 whether working or not; 60 to 64 only if not permanently retired and hasn't ceased an employment arrangement; never 65 or over.
Order: the notice of intent must be acknowledged before the split request, or the deduction is lost.
Ownership: once transferred, the split amount belongs to the spouse. It's part of their balance, it's preserved, and they can only access it when they meet a condition of release.
Caps: the split amount still counts towards the member's own concessional cap, not the spouse's.

detailed.example: $20,000 of concessional contributions last year: up to $17,000 can move to the spouse this year.

detailed.note: We may refuse a split that would leave the member's accumulation balance below $6,000. One request per financial year, received by 30 June.

items.general: Explain eligibility. Whether splitting makes sense is advice.

The split contributions belong to your spouse once they have been transferred to their account.

items.title: Carry-forward of unused cap
simple: Each year has a concessional (pre-tax) cap of $32,500. Any part you don't use can be carried forward for up to five years.
You can only use carried-forward amounts if your total super balance was under $500,000 on the previous 30 June.
Contributions fill this year's cap first, then the oldest unused amounts, so the amounts closest to expiring are used first.

standard.lead: How contributions fill the caps, in order:

standard: This year's general cap ($32,500) fills first.
Once it's full, unused amounts from earlier years are used, oldest year first. This happens automatically.
Anything over that is an excess contribution and may mean extra tax.

options.name: Eligibility
options.text: Total super balance under $500,000 on the previous 30 June.

options.name: Expiry
options.text: Each year's unused amount lasts five years, then it's gone.

standard.example: If you used $20,000 of a $32,500 cap, the $12,500 you didn't use is available for the next five years.

standard.note: The ATO tracks your available amounts in ATO online services. We can't see them.

detailed: Unused concessional cap can be carried forward for up to five years, then it expires.
To use it in a year, total super balance must have been under $500,000 on the previous 30 June.
The current year's general cap fills first.
Then unused amounts, oldest year first, applied automatically once the general cap is exceeded.
Anything beyond that is an excess concessional contribution: added to assessable income and taxed at marginal rates, less a 15% offset.

detailed.example: Unused amounts of $14,000 (2021-22) and $13,500 (2022-23), and $45,000 contributed this year: $32,500 fills this year's cap, then $12,500 comes from the 2021-22 amount. That leaves $1,500 from 2021-22 and all of 2022-23's for later.

detailed.note: The ATO, not UniSuper, works out what's available (ATO online services: Super, Information, Carry forward concessional contributions). Using it with personal contributions still needs a notice of intent.

items.title: Bring-forward of the after-tax cap
simple: The non-concessional (after-tax) cap is $130,000 a year.
If you're under 75, you can bring forward up to two future years' caps and put in up to $390,000 at once. Those future years' caps are then used up.
How much you can bring forward depends on your total super balance: from $1.97 million there's no bring-forward, and from $2.1 million the after-tax cap is nil.

Your total super balance on the previous 30 June decides how much you can put in:
Everything you put in during the period counts towards that total, until the period ends.

Once triggered, the period and its total are fixed for that period.

items.title: Preservation age and conditions of release
simple: Super is preserved: you can't take it out until you meet a condition of release.
For anyone under 60 today, preservation age is 60, so retiring before 60 doesn't release super.
The main conditions are retiring from 60, ending a job from 60, or turning 65. Before 60, only special grounds apply, such as severe financial hardship or a terminal illness.

head: Age
What releases super
rows: Retiring doesn't. Only special grounds: severe financial hardship, compassionate grounds, a terminal medical condition or permanent incapacity.
Retiring, or ending any job on or after 60, even if you keep working elsewhere. A TTR pension is also available while working.
Released, whether you're working or not.

standard: Preservation age is 60 for anyone born from 1 July 1964, which is everyone under 60 today.

standard.note: A member under 60 who says they've retired still can't access their super unless one of the special grounds applies.

detailed: Access needs a condition of release. The age-based ones depend on preservation age, which is 60 for anyone born on or after 1 July 1964.
Anyone under 60 today was born after 1 July 1964, so the older preservation ages of 55 to 59 only apply to members who are already over 60.

head: Condition
How it works
rows: Permanently retiring from the workforce on or after preservation age (60).
Ceasing an employment arrangement on or after 60 releases the balance at that point, even if the member keeps or starts another job.
Permanent incapacity, a terminal medical condition, severe financial hardship, compassionate grounds, death, or a balance under $200 when leaving an employer who contributed to UniSuper.

detailed: A TTR pension gives limited access from preservation age while still working.

detailed.note: Retiring before 60 isn't a condition of release for anyone currently under 60. Check the early access grounds instead.

items.general: Factual. Whether someone has 'retired' for super purposes can depend on their circumstances: check the rules.

retirement from the workforce on or after reaching your preservation age, which is currently age 60
ceasing an arrangement of employment on or after the age of 60, turning age 65, permanent incapacity, having an account balance of less than $200

items.title: Taxable and tax-free components
simple: Your super has two components: tax-free (mostly your after-tax contributions) and taxable (pre-tax contributions and earnings).
Every withdrawal takes from both in the same proportion. You can't choose.
From 60, withdrawals are tax-free, so the components mainly matter under 60 and for death benefits.

head: Component
Mostly made up of
rows: Employer contributions, salary sacrifice, deducted personal contributions, and earnings

standard: Every withdrawal takes from both in the same proportion as your whole balance. You can't choose.

standard.example: If 10% is tax-free, a $10,000 withdrawal is $1,000 tax-free and $9,000 taxable.

standard: From 60, withdrawals are tax-free, so the split doesn't affect you. It can still matter for a death benefit paid to someone who isn't a tax dependant.
detailed: Every benefit has a tax-free component and a taxable component.
Any lump sum must include both components in the same proportions as the whole benefit.

detailed.example: If 10% of the balance is tax-free, a $10,000 withdrawal under 60 is $1,000 tax-free and $9,000 taxable.

detailed: Only the taxable component can be taxed, and only under 60. From 60, withdrawals are tax-free.

detailed.note: Components still matter for death benefits to non-dependants: up to 17% on the taxed element. The member's actual components are on their statement.

items.general: Explain the components. The member's actual components are on their statement.

source.quote: Any lump sum withdrawal you make must include taxable and tax-free components in the same proportions as your entire benefit.

items.title: Binding, non-binding and reversionary nominations
simple: Super doesn't automatically form part of your estate, so you nominate who should receive it if you die. There are three types:

options.name: Binding
options.text: The Trustee must follow it.

options.name: Non-binding
options.text: A preference the Trustee considers.

options.name: Reversionary
options.text: For pensions: payments continue to that person.

standard: Super isn't automatically covered by your will, so a nomination tells the Trustee who should receive it. There are three types:

options.name: Binding
options.text: If it's valid when you die, the Trustee must pay the people you named, in your proportions.

options.name: Non-binding
options.text: A preference. The Trustee considers it, but decides.

options.name: Reversionary (pensions only)
options.text: Your pension keeps paying to that person instead of becoming a lump sum. It overrides any other nomination on that pension.

standard: You can only nominate dependants (spouse, children, financial dependants, interdependents) or your estate.

standard.note: With no valid nomination, the Trustee decides how to pay among your dependants and estate.

detailed: Without a valid nomination, the Trustee decides how to pay among dependants and the legal personal representative.

options.name: Binding (lapsing or non-lapsing)
options.text: Must be followed if valid and in effect at death: a lump sum in the nominated proportions.

options.name: Non-binding
options.text: Guides the Trustee's decision but doesn't bind it. Doesn't expire.

options.name: Reversionary (Flexi Pension, not BIS)
options.text: Income continues to that person. Overrides any other nomination on that pension, and can't be split.

detailed: Only dependants or the legal personal representative can be nominated.

detailed.note: Who counts as a dependant for tax is narrower: {{adult-children-tax:adult children usually aren't}}, so a lump sum to them may be taxed.

items.general: Explain the options. Which one suits someone's family and tax situation is advice.

source.quote: If the nomination is valid and still in effect at the date of your death, the Trustee must pay your account balance as a lump sum to the beneficiaries in the proportions you've nominated.

items.title: Lapsing and non-lapsing binding nominations
simple: Binding nominations come in two kinds: non-lapsing, which lasts until you change it, and lapsing, which expires after three years.
Non-lapsing can be done online. Lapsing needs a paper form signed in front of two witnesses.
An expired lapsing nomination is treated as non-binding.

Lapsing

standard.note: If it expires or is invalid, it's treated as non-binding. A paper form with no type ticked is lapsing.

detailed: Both kinds need: only dependants or the legal personal representative, exactly 100% allocated, and signed by the member (not a power of attorney).

source.quote: A valid binding death nomination (non-lapsing) won't expire unless you amend or revoke it, so it doesn't need to be confirmed or updated every three years.

items.title: When default cover starts
simple: Accumulation 1 members get default Death and TPD cover automatically, without health questions.
It starts once you're 25 and your balance reaches $6,000, with your employer's next contribution.
You can opt out before it starts so no premiums are charged.

standard.lead: Default Death and TPD cover starts automatically once both of these are true:

options.name: Age
options.text: You're 25 or older.

options.name: Balance
options.text: Your balance is at least $6,000.

standard: Once both are met, 10 units of cover start with your employer's next contribution, with no health questions. That contribution has to arrive within 180 days.
If you don't want it, opt out before it starts, so no premiums are deducted.

standard.note: Under 25 or under $6,000? You can still apply within 180 days of starting with an eligible employer, without health evidence.

options.name: Age
options.text: 25 or over.

options.name: Balance
options.text: At least $6,000.

detailed: Once both are met, cover starts on the date the next employer contribution is received, as long as it arrives within 180 days.
Default is 10 units of Death and TPD without health evidence, with Income Protection where it applies.
Members under 25 or under $6,000 can apply within 180 days of starting with an eligible employer, without health evidence.
Opting out before the start date means no premiums are deducted.

detailed.example: Someone who turns 25 in March with $7,000 would see cover start with their next pay's contribution.

items.general: Explain when cover starts. Whether to keep, change or cancel cover is the member's decision.

source.quote: Your Death and/or TPD cover (including any top-up cover) and Income Protection cover will start on the date we next receive an employer contribution into your Accumulation 1 account after you're aged 25 and have an account balance of at least $6,000

items.title: Why unitised cover goes down with age
simple: Unitised cover is bought in units. Each unit pays out an amount set by your age.
The cover per unit rises to a peak at 38, then falls as you get older.
Because the cover per unit falls, the cost per unit moves far less than the cover does, though it still changes with age.
So with the same number of units, the premium stays fairly even while your cover goes down.
standard: With unitised cover you hold a set number of units. Each unit's value is set by your age.

head: Unitised
Fixed
rows: Changes with age: peaks at 38, then falls
Death stays the same. TPD reduces each year from 61 to 70
Changes with age, but far less than the cover does

standard.example: One unit of Death cover for a man costs $8.12 a year at 30 and $11.56 at 60, while the cover it buys falls from $20,300 to $4,700. 10 units are worth $266,000 at 35 but $86,000 at 55.

standard: If you'd rather keep the same amount of Death cover, you can convert to fixed cover. Its cost still changes with age.

head: Unitised

Death stays the same. TPD reduces each year from 61 to 70
Changes with age, but far less than the cover does

detailed: Cover per unit peaks at $27,500 for death and TPD at age 38, then falls to $900 at 70. TPD stops at 70; Death cover continues to 74.

detailed.example: One unit of Death cover for a man costs $8.12 a year at 30 and $11.56 at 60, while the cover it buys falls from $20,300 to $4,700. 10 units are worth $266,000 at 35 but $86,000 at 55.

detailed: Premiums in the PDS table are illustrative annual examples per unit. The actual cost is worked out from rates per $1,000 of cover, and Personal Account members also apply an occupation factor.

detailed.note: Which type suits is a personal decision.

items.general: Explain how it works. Whether unitised or fixed suits someone is a personal decision.

The amount of cover and cost will change as you get older.
It also provides illustrative examples of the annual premiums for one unit of Death cover or one unit of TPD cover based on age and sex at birth.
From age 61 to 70, the amount of TPD cover you hold will automatically reduce proportionately each year.
Actual cost of insurance is calculated by premium rates per $1,000 of cover.

items.title: Inactive accounts and insurance
simple: An account is inactive if it hasn't received a contribution or rollover for 16 months in a row.
Insurance on an inactive account stops, unless you've told us you want to keep it.
If an inactive account is also under $6,000, it may be transferred to the ATO.
standard: An account is inactive after 16 consecutive months with no contribution or rollover. Two things can then happen:

options.name: Insurance stops
options.text: Unless you've told us you want to keep it.

options.name: Account may go to the ATO
options.text: If the balance is also under $6,000. The ATO then tries to combine it with another active account in your name.

standard: These are legal rules to stop small, forgotten accounts being eroded by fees and premiums.
detailed: Inactive means no contribution or rollover for 16 consecutive months.

options.name: Insurance
options.text: Ends at 16 months unless the member elected to keep it before then.

options.name: Low balance
options.text: Inactive accounts under $6,000 are transferred to the ATO unless an exception applies. The ATO consolidates them into an active account where it can.

detailed.example: If contributions stopped in January 2026, cover would stop around May 2027 unless the member had asked to keep it.

detailed.note: Keeping cover is the member's decision.

items.general: Factual. Whether to keep cover is the member's decision.

source.quote: Your account hasn't received a contribution or rollover for 16 consecutive months, and prior to that you didn't elect to keep cover
